subtopics.title: Factorise trinomials with a = 1
subtopics.exposition: Factorising is the reverse of calculating the product of factors. A difference of squares, a^2-b^2, can be written in factorised form as (a+b)(a-b), because (a+b)(a-b)=a^2-b^2. The x^2 term in the quadratic is the product of the x-terms in each bracket. In (x+2)(x+3) = x^2+5x+6, the 6 in the quadratic is the product of the 2 and 3 in the brackets. The middle term of the quadratic is the sum of two terms. If c is positive, then the factors of c must be either both positive or both negative. If c is negative, only one of the factors of c is negative, the other one being positive. To factorise a quadratic, we find the factors which, when multiplied together, equal the original quadratic. If a quadratic is made up of a difference of squares, the factors can be written down immediately; many quadratics do not fall into this kind, and a more general method is needed to factorise them. Multiplying two binomials gives a quadratic: (x+2)(x+3) = x^2+3x+2x+6 = x^2+5x+6. Looking at this opposite process helps us learn how to factorise. To factorise x^2+5x+6, first write down the two brackets with an x in each bracket and space for the remaining terms. Next decide upon the factors of 6. Since 6 is positive, the possible combinations are 1 and 6, 2 and 3, -1 and -6, or -2 and -3. Next, expand each set of brackets to see which option gives the correct middle term. Expanding the four options gives: (x+1)(x+6) = x^2+7x+6; (x-1)(x-6) = x^2-7x+6; (x+2)(x+3) = x^2+5x+6; (x-2)(x-3) = x^2-5x+6. Option 3, (x+2)(x+3), gives the correct middle term, so it is the correct factorisation of x^2+5x+6.

subtopics.title: Factorise trinomials with a ≠ 1
subtopics.exposition: Write down two brackets with an x in each bracket and space for the remaining terms. Write down a set of factors for a and for c. Write down a set of options for the possible factors of the quadratic using the factors of a and c. Expand all the options to see which one gives the correct middle term bx. To factorise 3x^2+2x-1, the possible factors for a are 1 and 3. In 3x^2+2x-1, c is negative; the possible factors for c are -1 and 1. Using the factors of a and c there are two possible options for 3x^2+2x-1: (x-1)(3x+1) and (x+1)(3x-1). Expanding the two options gives 3x^2-2x-1 for (x-1)(3x+1) and 3x^2+2x-1 for (x+1)(3x-1); the second has the correct middle term +2x. Check the solution by multiplying the factors: (x+1)(3x-1) = 3x^2-x+3x-1 = 3x^2+2x-1. Write the final answer: 3x^2+2x-1 = (x+1)(3x-1).

subtopics.title: Take out common factor first
subtopics.exposition: In a quadratic expression of the form ax^2+bx, x is a common factor in both terms, so ax^2+bx factorises as x(ax+b). For example, 8y^2+4y factorises as 4y(2y+1), taking out the common factor 4y. First take out any common factor in the coefficients of the terms of the expression, to obtain an expression of the form ax^2+bx+c where a, b and c have no common factors and a is positive.

claims.claim: Factorising is the reverse of calculating the product of factors.
To factorise a quadratic, we find the factors which, when multiplied together, equal the original quadratic.
In a quadratic expression of the form ax^2+bx, x is a common factor in both terms, so ax^2+bx factorises as x(ax+b).
For example, 8y^2+4y factorises as 4y(2y+1), taking out the common factor 4y.
A difference of squares, a^2-b^2, can be written in factorised form as (a+b)(a-b), because (a+b)(a-b)=a^2-b^2.
If a quadratic is made up of a difference of squares, the factors can be written down immediately; many quadratics do not fall into this kind, and a more general method is needed to factorise them.
Multiplying two binomials gives a quadratic: (x+2)(x+3) = x^2+3x+2x+6 = x^2+5x+6. Looking at this opposite process helps us learn how to factorise.
The x^2 term in the quadratic is the product of the x-terms in each bracket.
In (x+2)(x+3) = x^2+5x+6, the 6 in the quadratic is the product of the 2 and 3 in the brackets.
The middle term of the quadratic is the sum of two terms.
To factorise x^2+5x+6, first write down the two brackets with an x in each bracket and space for the remaining terms.
Next decide upon the factors of 6. Since 6 is positive, the possible combinations are 1 and 6, 2 and 3, -1 and -6, or -2 and -3.
Next, expand each set of brackets to see which option gives the correct middle term.
Expanding the four options gives: (x+1)(x+6) = x^2+7x+6; (x-1)(x-6) = x^2-7x+6; (x+2)(x+3) = x^2+5x+6; (x-2)(x-3) = x^2-5x+6.
Option 3, (x+2)(x+3), gives the correct middle term, so it is the correct factorisation of x^2+5x+6.
The process of factorising a quadratic is mostly trial and error, but there are some strategies that can be used to ease the process.
First take out any common factor in the coefficients of the terms of the expression, to obtain an expression of the form ax^2+bx+c where a, b and c have no common factors and a is positive.
Write down two brackets with an x in each bracket and space for the remaining terms.
Write down a set of factors for a and for c.
Write down a set of options for the possible factors of the quadratic using the factors of a and c.
Expand all the options to see which one gives the correct middle term bx.
If c is positive, then the factors of c must be either both positive or both negative.
If c is negative, only one of the factors of c is negative, the other one being positive.
Once you get an answer, always multiply out the brackets again to make sure it really works.
To factorise 3x^2+2x-1, the possible factors for a are 1 and 3.
In 3x^2+2x-1, c is negative; the possible factors for c are -1 and 1.
Using the factors of a and c there are two possible options for 3x^2+2x-1: (x-1)(3x+1) and (x+1)(3x-1).
Expanding the two options gives 3x^2-2x-1 for (x-1)(3x+1) and 3x^2+2x-1 for (x+1)(3x-1); the second has the correct middle term +2x.
Check the solution by multiplying the factors: (x+1)(3x-1) = 3x^2-x+3x-1 = 3x^2+2x-1.
Write the final answer: 3x^2+2x-1 = (x+1)(3x-1).
